extracted_information: Windows Service Hardening is a set of security features introduced in Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista designed to reduce the attack surface of services and thwart malware and intruders. It addresses the historical vulnerability of Windows services, which were often targets due to running by default with high privileges and network communication capabilities. The Blaster worm is cited as an example of malware exploiting highly privileged services (Windows RPC service).

Components.Name: Session 0 Isolation
Components.Description: Ensures that only Windows services run in Session 0 (the console session), which is marked as non-interactive. User applications run in a separate session (Session 1) to prevent interference with highly privileged services. This prevents services from directly communicating with users (e.g., creating dialog boxes).

Technical Details.Previous Behavior (Pre-Vista): Session 0 ran services and interactive user applications, posing a risk of malicious applications interfering with highly privileged services.
Technical Details.Workaround for Legacy Services: Interactive Services Detection service (ui0detect.exe), turned off by default, can be enabled to allow legacy interactive services to interact with users by generating a user approval prompt. This is insecure and temporary, planned for removal in future Windows releases. It only works for GUI-based services, not console/command-prompt services.
Technical Details.Developer Solution: Developers can use secure interprocess communications (e.g., named pipes, RPCs) for Session 0 services to interact with the desktop.
Technical Details.At command (at.exe): Cannot execute interactive programs in Session 0 in Server 2008/Vista due to non-interactive nature.

Components.Name: Least-Privilege Restrictions
Components.Description: Guarantees services receive only necessary privileges. Default permissions and rights for built-in services were re-evaluated and reduced. Many services previously running as Local System now run as LocalService or NetworkService (less-privileged accounts introduced in XP SP2/Windows 2003).

Technical Details.Mechanism: Service Control Manager (SCM) assigns privileges based on the 'RequiredPrivileges' registry entry of a service. Only specified privileges are enabled in the access token of the process hosting the service. SCM enforces these settings during runtime, preventing additional privileges from being granted.
Technical Details.Example: For a service 'MyService' needing only 'Backup files and directories' right: `sc privs MyService SeBackupPrivilege`
Technical Details.Observation Tool: Windows Sysinternals Process Explorer (Security tab shows enabled/disabled rights in access token).

Components.Name: Service-Specific SIDs
Components.Description: Each service can have a unique SID, allowing administrators and developers to use these SIDs in Access Control Lists (ACLs) to protect service-specific resources. This avoids the need for custom Windows accounts for each service, reducing management overhead and leveraging automated password management for built-in accounts.

Technical Details.Purpose: To grant access to specific resources solely for a service, rather than all services running under a shared account (e.g., LocalSystem, NetworkService).
Technical Details.Nature of SIDs: Local (machine-level), automatically computed and linked to the service name.
Technical Details.SID Format: S-1-5-80-{SHA-1(service name in uppercase)}. Identical across Vista/Server 2008 machines for the same service.

Components.Name: Write-Restricted SIDs and Tokens
Components.Description: A more secure variant of service-specific SIDs, specifically preventing a compromised service from writing to non-service-related resources that its service account (e.g., LocalService) could otherwise access. These SIDs restrict access and cannot broaden it.

Technical Details.SID Type Setting: Set a service's SID type property to 'restricted'. Developers can include 'WRITE_RESTRICTED' flag in service code.
Technical Details.Access-Control Check (Two Passes): 1. Typical ACL pass based on resource permissions and hosting process access token. 2. Extra pass explicitly checks if resource permissions grant explicit write access to the service-specific SID, 'Logon SID', 'Everyone', or 'WRITE RESTRICTED' SIDs. Both passes must succeed for write access.
Technical Details.Impact: Requires explicit granting of write permissions to resources the service needs to modify when a write-restricted SID is enabled (e.g., Windows Firewall's write-restricted SID requires explicit write access to %System%LogFiles\Firewall folder).
Technical Details.Example: Windows Firewall service (mpssvc.exe) has a write-restricted SID.

Components.Name: Restricted Network Access
Components.Description: Allows developers to define restrictions on a service's network access, whether inbound or outbound. These restrictions are enforced regardless of Windows Firewall status and are evaluated before Firewall rules.

Technical Details.Distinction from Windows Firewall: Not integrated with Windows Firewall; enforced even if Firewall is off. Cannot be configured via 'Windows Firewall with Advanced Security' MMC snap-in or `netsh advfirewall`.
Technical Details.Purpose: Can only restrict (deny) access, not grant (allow).
Technical Details.Configuration: Must be defined programmatically using INetFwServiceRestriction and INetFwRule programming interfaces.
Technical Details.Subkeys: StaticSystem (predefined restrictions for built-in services, can be modified with administrator privileges in registry), Configurable (custom restrictions).

references: Mark E. Russinovich and David A. Solomon, Microsoft Windows Internals, Microsoft Press, 2005 (new edition scheduled for November 2008).
Microsoft white paper 'Impact of Session 0 Isolation on Services and Drivers in Windows Vista' at www.microsoft.com/whdc/system/vista/services.mspx
'Windows Vista's Take on Least Privilege,' October 2006, InstantDoc ID 93300.
